en: Having explained *bodhicitta*, he says "Now," and so forth, in order to explain this very great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—which was indicated immediately prior—along with its method.
It is called "determination" (*nirṇaya*) because it has been determined; it is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), which is great bliss.
To the question, "In what way is this the definitive meaning? he replies, "Because of its equality."

Because it is of one flavor with the bodhicitta of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) for all sentient beings—that is to say, because it is identical with it—what is the basis for its realization? It is the triangular *bhaga*, the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*), the emanation-lotus (*nirmāṇapadma*), and so forth; for it is in this [place] that the three channels (*lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī*) exist.

Because the nature of all sublime qualities, such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), is present here in their excellence, it is "possessed of a sublime form" (*udārarūpin*) through its connection with them. It is the support for the undifferentiated great bliss shared by all, including the gods and demigods from Brahmā downwards.

[Objection: "But surely in the Sūtras, Tantras, and so forth, it is only the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that is stated to be the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and not Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*. To this he says: "That" refers to the determination. It is endowed with the nature of conventional forms, such as color and shape. This is what is meant: conventional [phenomena] such as blue and so forth have bliss as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). As it is said in the *Hevajratantra* (II.ii.):
Bliss is blue, bliss is yellow, bliss is like the *kunda* flower, and so forth.

Bliss is the *bodhicitta*, and that itself is the *prajñāpāramitā*. For this very reason, in some places the woman (*yoṣit*) is called the *prajñāpāramitā*, and in others the *dharmodaya* and so on; therefore, this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Because that [bliss] transcends objects, is in the ultimate sense free from the superimposition of objects, and abides as the very identity within the heart-mind of all living beings—living beings being composed of that.

[Objection: But how can great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which is not experienced at the time of its actual departure from reality (*tattva*), be said to be the essence of the minds of all sentient beings? [Reply: It is by virtue of their *capacity* for the experience of great bliss. We shall explain this in detail. [Objection: If that is so, why is enlightenment (*bodhi*) attained through the extensive practice of the six perfections consisting of ritual action (*kriyāmaya*) based on the Vehicle of Perfections (*pāramitānaya*), rather than through the Mantra Vehicle (*mantranaya*)? [Reply: If that [enlightenment] consists of great bliss, it begins from the stage of Joy (*muditābhūmi*). Thus he says.

"What," and so forth. For what purpose, in detail—that is, at length—[is this taught] for Vajragarbha, who possesses sharp wisdom? For one of sharp wisdom [realizes that] within this *bodhicitta* the perfections (*pāramitā*) are condensed; or rather, "condensation" (*saṃkṣepa*) means the act of condensing. Therefore, [this teaching] follows [for him], because the ten perfections, which are included within *bodhicitta*, are brought to fulfillment through cultivation. Consequently, however, the performance of the welfare of others occurs effortlessly (*anābhoga*).

Buddhahood, mastery of the ten stages, the state of being fully awakened, the attainment of the path of distinction, the state of holding the vajra, mastery of the eleventh stage, the state of a universal monarch, and being the leader of infinite emanated maṇḍala-circles.

"Countless" refers to the *koṭis* of eons (*kalpas*). Here, "eon" means a great eon (*mahākalpa*). For instance, the time required for humans with a lifespan of ten years to increase until their lifespan reaches eighty thousand years, and then decrease back down to ten years—that period of increase and decrease is an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*). Eighty intermediate eons constitute a great eon. A great eon is [thus defined].

Thus, when great eons (*mahākalpa*) reach a numerical value that has passed through sixty places, they are called "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*). When these very incalculables are turned back and counted again, there are three incalculables. By means of these three, those who are endowed with the method of the perfections (*pāramitānaya*) attain [the goal].

It is attained through incalculable aeons (*kalpāsaṃkhyeya*). Among these, by the first incalculable aeon, starting from the stage of equipment (*sambhārabhūmi*) up to the first [bodhisattva] stage is accomplished; by the second, the six stages beginning with the Vimalā; and by the third, starting from the Acalā stage up to the stage of a perfectly awakened Buddha (*samyaksambuddhabhūmi*). Even for those possessing great heroism, it is unattainable in ten million aeons; rather, full awakening (*abhisambodhi*) occurs in the very second incalculable aeon.
The word "tvam" (you) is supplemented by "yathā" (just as). The meaning is: "just as you attain Buddhahood and so forth in this very life."

This has been said: just as for a Bodhisattva following the vehicle of the perfections (*pāramitānāyika*) who exerts himself with great vigor, many eons (*kalpa*) are brought to an end—as occurred for our Blessed One Śākyamuni when, while he was a Bodhisattva, nine eons were bypassed through his propitiation of the Buddha Upatiṣya—so too, for one who exerts himself with extremely great effort, there occurs the bypassing of even many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.

Likewise, for those who strive with unsurpassed, ultimate, and great exertion and through specific skillful means (*upāya-viśeṣa*), there occurs a reversal [of the process] even within two incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), such that they attain perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*) in as few as several births within a single eon, or even in this very life.

For this very reason, he says: "by which" (referring to) the intention that it is produced by skillful means such as the action-seal (*karma-mudrā*); "true bliss" refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

For this very reason, since the stage of the Vajradhara, which is of the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), is established right here, the superiority of the Mantra system over the Pāramitā systems has been explained in detail.

Now, one might object: "In this context, great bliss is said to arise solely from the yoga with a mudrā; and that [yoga] occurs by the power of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, and from that, passion and the rest arise. If these are not causes of bondage, then all living beings would be liberated without effort.
To this he replies, "Delusion," and so on.

That which, through its association with certain factors (dharma), prevents one from seeing things as they truly are, and causes one to superimpose a non-existent intrinsic nature upon entities—whether as a person (pudgala) or as a phenomenon (dharma)—or to superimpose non-existence [where it does not exist], is ignorance (avidyā), delusion (moha); delusion is the opposite of knowledge (vidyā). Knowledge, however, is the thorough comprehension of the two truths; it is untainted cognition (anāsrava-jñāna) having the intrinsic nature of phenomena as its object.
Hatred (dveṣa) is resentment (pratigha) or malice (vyāpāda); that is to say, it is the state of harboring ill-will toward sentient beings.

Attachment (*rāga*) is *anunaya*, the determination of craving, and clinging. It is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) that is the cause for the transformation of the nature of the mind in one who considers oneself superior to others or equal to them; this is defiled pride (*māna*). Envy (*īrṣyā*) is the distress caused by the virtues of others.

They are called "defilements" (*saṃkleśa*) because they defile sentient beings. The term "by their own limbs" (*svāṅgakena*) is used in the singular to denote the class. Those [limbs] by which [beings] are bound to themselves, and those which afflict them with their own parts, are as follows: ignorance (*avidyā*) is that which is unwholesome (*aśubha*) belonging specifically to the desire realm; and formations (*saṃskāra*) are wholesome (*śubha*) contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma belonging to the three realms. Conditioned by formations is consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is the mind at the moment of linking rebirth in the mother's womb, or the five aggregates. Conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

In that regard, at the stage of rebirth-linking within the mother’s womb, there are four formless aggregates—feeling and the rest—as well as derived matter based on the primary elements, according to their occurrence. That very state is called *kalala*. Gradually, it passes through the stages of *arbuda*, *ghana*, *peśī*, *praśākhā*, and so forth. When name-and-form has reached growth, it becomes the condition for the six sense bases, beginning with the eye.

From the maturation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the presence of an object, contact (*sparśa*) arises; it consists of the conjunction of the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness. From that arises feeling (*vedanā*), which takes the form of experiencing pleasure, pain, or equanimity in accordance with that contact. From that arises craving (*tṛṣṇā*): a desire for non-separation from pleasant feeling, a desire for separation from painful feeling, and, in turn, a desire for neither-pleasure-nor-pain.

From craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises grasping (*upādāna*), which is the desire and attachment (*chanda-rāga*) toward sense-pleasures and so forth. What is the distinction between craving and grasping? Craving is, without distinction, the delight in renewed existence; grasping is that same delight with specific distinction. Alternatively, craving is the state of being distant [from the result], while grasping is the state of being near [to it]. Consequently, when the seed of the formative forces (*saṃskāra-bīja*) is moistened by craving and grasping and is oriented toward the production of its fruit, that karma is called "existence" (*bhava*). From existence arises birth (*jāti*), through the sequence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) up to sensation (*vedanā*).

For one who is born, aging, death, and so forth occur; thus there are twelve other factors for one who is transmigrating. One who touches these various states—neither one who dies in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), nor one belonging to the realms of form or formlessness (*rūpārūpyāvacara*)—has ignorance and formations as his past birth; consciousness up to becoming as his present [birth]; and birth, aging, and death as his future [birth]. In this way, the twelvefold dependent origination is to be understood as having three paths.

Ignorance, craving, and grasping constitute the path of afflictions (*kleśavartman*); formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*) constitute the path of karma (*karmavartman*); and the remaining members constitute the path of maturation (*vipākavartman*). As it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna in the *Ratnāvalī* (1.36):
"This wheel of saṃsāra consists of these three paths, which are without beginning, middle, or end."
Resembling a circle of fire, it revolves with mutual causality.

Thus [it is said]. Herein, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are primary; for it is through the sovereignty of the afflictions that karma projects rebirth. This is because one who has seen the truths does not project a future existence, even though karma still exists. And so it is stated in the *Mañjuśrī-tantra*:

Furthermore, O hosts of gods, those who know all mantras understand that all phenomena are dependently originated. It occurs to them: "These phenomena are thus empty, like an illusion, unstable," and so forth; "their arising is perceived, their duration is perceived, and their cessation is perceived; these formative forces arise with ignorance as their condition," and so forth; "in this way, there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering."

Therefore, one of a wise nature should strive for the abandonment of ignorance. Through the cessation of ignorance, these phenomena dependent upon non-knowing cease; through the abandonment of non-knowing, the afflictions do not manifest, the destinies are ceased, and the causes of saṃsāra come to an end. One draws near to nirvāṇa.
By means of the effortless manifestation of the intrinsic nature, the movements, births, deaths, and transitions of saṃsāra, one enters into the accomplishment of all mantras.

For this very reason, he says: "deluded by the afflictions" (*kleśaiḥ vimohitāḥ*). Since these are the causes of bondage, he says that these afflictions must be removed, beginning with the words "for this reason" (*ataḥ*) and so forth. "Yukti" means yoga; it refers to the meditative absorption of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya-samāpatti*), which is to say, the *bodhicitta*.

Regarding the phrase "separation from suffering" (*duḥkhaviyogam*): it is a collective compound (*samāhāra*) consisting of both "suffering" and "separation from desired worldly and supramundane goals."
[The compound of distributive analysis (*paryāya-dvandva*): How are the afflictions (*kleśa*) refuted by reasoning? To this he says: "Having become conditions," and so forth.

Passion and the other afflictions, when purified in the form of the *bodhicitta*, abandon their state as passion and so forth; they then become the auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) for the present fruit. And the *bodhicitta* is the cause as the substantial cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). Thus, it is stated that there is no union with a consort (*mudrā-yoga*) by means of passion and the like, nor do passion and the like arise from that [union].

But even so, how can the yoga of mudrās and the like be conducive to the attainment of the highest good? Because of a specific kind of superimposition (*samāropa*). For superimposition is of two kinds: that which consists of reality (*tattvarūpa*) and that which does not consist of reality (*atattvarūpa*). In this regard, there is no fault, because a superimposition consisting of reality—such as the superimposition of [the consort] Mātrā and others—serves as a means to awakening through a gradual succession.
But would there not be a contradiction, since for some the experience of the female form is also prohibited?

For action is of two kinds, distinguished as that which is originated (*samutthāpya*) and that which originates (*samutthāpaka*). Among these, all bodily and vocal action is that which is originated, while mental action is that which originates. And this [mental action] is of two kinds: that consisting of non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth, and its opposite. Among these, all bodily and vocal action originated by greed (*lobha*) and so forth is unwholesome (*akuśala*), and that is prohibited. All [action] originated by non-greed and so forth is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).

And the yogin, joined with the non-dual yoga of Mahāmudrā, beholds the entire world as consisting of non-attachment and so forth. Therefore, even while engaged in all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), he is of a virtuous nature because of the non-apprehension of anything unwholesome. For this very reason, it is said in the *Guhyendutilaka* and other tantras:
"There is nothing whatsoever that should not be done by one whose mind is endowed with wisdom and skillful means."
Always remaining free from doubt, enjoy the fivefold objects of desire.
For one whose bodhicitta is firm and whose mind is free from attachment, no doubt should be entertained; for such a person, this will certainly succeed.
He who, having understood the reality with effort, cultivates resolute conviction, succeeds; otherwise, he falls into the great hell.
Thus it is said. And it is stated in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (*Kāśyapaparivarta*):

"For example, Kāśyapa, just as a heap of refuse is beneficial in fields of rice, so too are the afflictions (*kleśa*) beneficial for a bodhisattva. For example, Kāśyapa, just as poison that is counteracted by mantras and medicines does not cause one to fall [into ruin], so too a bodhisattva endowed with wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) is not caused to fall by the afflictions."
For this very reason, it is said that the transformation of pleasure born of touch is the cause for the unsurpassed fruit.
And so it is stated in the *Vajraḍāka-tantra*:
[Q/R *Vajraḍāka*]

And thus, even by means of such illusion-like entities, through the dedication of the bliss produced from a sublime enjoyment, when these [entities], by the power of the practice of sublime meditation, produce an effect such as sublime mental well-being and so forth, and thereby function as the cause for attaining the unsurpassed fruit, then, O Goddess, there is no fault whatsoever.
For this very reason, it is stated in other tantras— such as the *Kālacakra-sādhana* and others— that the gift of desire yields greater fruit than any other gift.
As it is said in the *Paramādya-tantra*:
"By enjoying all objects of desire as one wishes, [the practice] is to be cultivated."
Through union with one's own presiding deity, one indeed gives birth to both oneself and others;
even unwholesome things should be given, for they provide all desired pleasures.
But for the sake of fulfilling all the hopes of both oneself and others.
Thus it was said by the Noble One:
"In some cases, even that which is seen to be unwholesome is considered wholesome by the wise. (Āryadeva, *Catuḥśataka*, Chapter 8)
Is it not the case that, by virtue of disease, everything indeed becomes known as medicine?
Thus it has been said by the Blessed One:
"For one who has conviction in phenomena as being like an illusion, the enjoyment of all things is appropriate."
And it is said in the *Sarvadevasamāgama-tantra*:
"By those very things by which the foolish are bound, the wise play here."
By means of the yoga that is completely filled with *sattva*, or otherwise like a lamp,
one who is always and in every state possessed of fearless *sattva* will not incur bondage, even while engaged in all forms of conduct.
For those who perceive all this as empty in form with an eye of emptiness, and who remain free from conceptual construction, fearlessness shall arise.
Regarding the question "Of the virtuous?"—
it is for this very reason that it was said [in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* by Asaṅga, in the section on primordial wisdom]:
Affliction has become a factor of enlightenment, and cyclic existence has attained the nature of peace;
therefore, because they possess such great skillful means, the sons of the Conquerors are indeed inconceivable.
Thus, it is established that the objects such as form (*rūpa*), when embraced by wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*) and being enjoyed, bring about a distinguished fruit.
What is that distinguished fruit? He says: "That which has become the fruit," and so forth.

This very cause is perceived as existing at the ultimate limit of the excellence of the direct realization of the nature of the bodhicitta consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). It is "to be characterized" (*lakṣya*) as the vision of stainless and immeasurable realities. By this, the fruit of both "omniscience through application" (*upayuktasarvajñatva*) and "omniscience of all things" (*sarvasarvajñatva*) is stated.

Now, one might ask: "In other tantras and here as well, the pacification of delusion and the other afflictions through Vairocana and the others has been taught; why then is it said to be 'by means of wisdom and method'? To this he replies: "By whichever [means]... Beings who have become [afflicted] by the nature of Vairocana and the others are to be purified through the cessation of their afflictions; those very ones, Vairocana and the rest, are the bearers of the essential form of that very Blessed One, the Vajra of Bodhicitta.

Just as the fires of the *dakṣiṇāgni*, *gārhapatya*, *āhavanīya*, and so forth, though distinct, are all of the very nature of fire in that they burn the fuel—such as the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), rags, and other impurities; so too, by virtue of the dispositions of those to be trained (*vineya*), this drama of Vairocana and the others is the manifestation of the Victor himself, the Lord of Great Bliss (*mahāsukhanātha*). As he will say: "Wherein the Lord of Great Bliss dances, for the sake of dancing with manifold aesthetic flavors."
It is "delightful" because it is a place of joyful attachment for those who possess resolute faith (*adhimukti*) toward it;
it is "divine" because it is the means for attaining purity.

Therefore, this very one is the Protector (*nātha*), because he has abandoned both types of obscurations along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanāvaraṇadvaya*); he is both pure and characterized.
Even those aggregates such as form (*rūpaskandha*) which are resolved upon as having the nature of Vairocana and the others, they too are this very [wisdom].

Yet, it is this alone that is capable of slaying the enemy of delusion and so forth; he says "even by way of the essential nature of Vairocana and the others," beginning with "delusion" and so on. The connection is: "it slays delusion. Vairocana is the purification of delusion (*moha*); Akṣobhya is the purification of hatred (*dveṣa*); Amitābha is the purification of passion (*rāga*); Ratnasambhava is the purification of pride (*māna*); and Amoghasiddhi is the purification of envy (*īrṣyā*).
"Vajradhr̥k. Regarding this, the *Samājottara* states: "The five weapons (*heti*) and the *veti* are designated as 'vajra'."
Retention is declared as *dhṛk*; the consciousness of the mind is *Vajradhṛk*.

Thus: *heti* means loss (*hāni*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); *veti* means finding (*vitti*), which is gnosis (*jñāna*). The meaning is that the five gnoses, whose nature is emptiness, are the *vajra*. For this very reason, the *vajra* with five prongs on both sides symbolizes that. Retention (*dhāraṇa*) and the retainer (*dhāraka*), which is consciousness (*vijñāna*), is called *dhṛk*. Therefore, in the *utpannakrama*, the mind (*manas*)—the *bodhicitta*—is called the "Holder of the Vajra" (*Vajradhṛk*).
And so it has been said: "Pure intellect (*dhī*), resembling the moon, is designated as the *vajra*."
Thus [it is said].
And because it crushes all the wicked, it is the indivisible penetration;
I am the Vajra of all Buddhas, I am the firm Bodhicitta.

And thus it is said. Furthermore, he is the Vajradhara because he holds the vajra that illuminates that [reality] through the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*). How is it that the purification of delusion and so forth constitutes Vajrasattva? Because of the passage beginning, "For the sake of the purification of that form" (144v/290). For this very reason, these five families, Vairocana and the others, are [emanations] of Vajradhara alone, since they radiate forth in the form of Akṣobhya. This was stated in the *Samājottara* (the *Guhyasamājatantra*).

The lineage (*kula*) is declared to be the succession (*anvaya*); that which is the beginning of the succession is called the "origin" (*ādi*). That which is indestructible and unarisen is proclaimed as the Lord (*nātha*).

Thus: *anvaya* (lineage) is the continuity (*anuvṛtti*) of some primordial [principle]. For this very reason, he says: "The primordial is called the lineage. But what is this? He says: "That which is indestructible," and so forth.

However, how can Akṣobhya and the others—who are of the nature of the purification of the aggregates such as consciousness—belong to the families of hatred and the rest? To this, the answer is found in the *Samājottara* (the *Guhyasamājatantra*).
Consciousness is declared to be hatred for those who hate, due to the duality of cause and effect;
form is known as delusion because its nature is that of a dull bondage;
and sensation is called intoxication and pride because its nature is egoism.
The perception known as "striking" is characterized by passion for the self and the inability to control the object;
however, the mental formation (*saṃskāra*) is always jealousy, driven by a mind impelled through dependent origination.
But the intrinsic nature of the mind of awakening arises everywhere throughout existence.

Thus: consciousness (*vijñāna*), which has the form of the two and five hogs, is hatred (*dveṣa*) because it serves as the antidote to the adversaries, that is, the obscurations. Form (*rūpa*), however, is delusion (*moha*) because its nature is insentient and because its nature is bondage. Its nature as bondage exists because form is the object of clinging. Feeling (*vedanā*) has the nature of the mind (*mānasvabhāva*), because from feelings such as pleasure arises the manifestation of the conceit "I am happy" and so forth. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is "the self consisting of passion"; perception consists of passion.

Because [ignorance] has the characteristic of non-attachment to objects (*vastu*), while [formative forces] have the characteristic of attachment to objects due to the grasping of the characteristics of objects; and because formative forces (*saṃskāra*) have envy as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), since they proceed by way of being impelled—by virtue of being dependently originated and having an impelled form through causes and conditions—they are called "formative forces" because they function impelled by causes. Furthermore, since envy itself has the nature of being impelled, formative forces possess the nature of envy.
Their belonging to the Vajradhara family has been established, but not their identity with that [Vajradhara] essence; thus he says: "the intrinsic nature."

Is that [nature] then merely purity? To this he says: "Arising everywhere in existence. The meaning is that their such nature flows continuously throughout the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). For this very reason, it is stated in that same [text], the *Guhyasamājatantra* (also known as the *Samājottara*):
Desire is said to be the mind when it is accompanied by passion, hatred, and delusion;
the commitment (samaya) is like the universe, facing toward the fruit born of karma.

Thus: "The pledge (samaya) resembling the universe. That mind which appears as the universe, being brought together as appropriate by Rāgavajra and the others, and which is this fruit born of karma that has arrived as supreme bliss—that is called "desire" (kāma). For it is solely through the power of karma that a mind arises in various forms conducive to passion (rāga) and so forth. And that is the "desire" of all yogins, because it is conducive to Rāgavajra and the others.

For this very reason, Dveṣavajra and the others are said to be the supreme state of union with Mahāmudrā. Furthermore, these [deities] such as Dveṣavajra become the ultimate reality that radiates forth for the yogin who consists of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and is by nature free from desire. However, in this context, it is not the actual physical forms whose functions are hatred and so forth that are thus generated, but rather the completely purified hatred and so forth.
As for what is stated in some places—“internally cool as frost, yet externally harsh,” and so on—that refers to those who are impure.

Furthermore, although hatred and the like are taught for the sake of destroying hatred and so forth, that too is with reference to the absence of impure forms within the objective support that consists of their pure form.

And as for what is said for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings belonging to the families of hatred and so forth, that too is because, having pervaded them with those very forms, one practices accordingly toward beginners; by remaining oneself in such a state, one establishes others in that same state. If these are the five families, how then will loving-kindness and the rest be included here? Because they have a virtuous nature.

For instance, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the desire to bestow happiness upon sentient beings, or a mind that is affectionate. Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the desire to remove suffering, or a mind that seeks their welfare. Joy (*muditā*) is the aspect of delighting in the prosperity of others, or the desire for them not to be separated from happiness. Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the state of indifference toward all phenomena because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), or an unshakable mind. Even equanimity toward the eight worldly concerns possesses the characteristic of equanimity and becomes completely pure precisely because of that very lack of intrinsic nature. In this way, it is quite evident that these [four immeasurables] take the form of the absence of delusion and so forth.

For this very reason, Locanā and the others, whose intrinsic nature consists of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth, are described by terms such as "delusion-delight" (*moharati*) and so on in the *Samāja* and other tantras. Furthermore, it has already been established through the aforementioned reasoning that hatred (*dveṣa*) and the rest are wholesome (*kuśala*). Therefore, when these wholesome factors radiate as loving-kindness and the like—which are themselves wholesome by nature—they are included within those [qualities] such as loving-kindness.

Regarding the "five cognitions": therein, the *suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna* (cognition of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena) is the perfection of the realization of the *dharmadhātu*—which consists of both compassion and wisdom—liberated from the two obscurations along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanāvaraṇa*). It arises from the culmination of the excellence of cultivation regarding the actual reality (*bhūtārtha*), which is the perfection of abandonment and realization. Because it accords with the actual reality, it is a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by a vivid appearance; and because it is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous, it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is the Blessed One, the omniscient one who has attained his goal.

The *ādarśajñāna* (mirror-like wisdom) is that in which the three realms of existence, down to every single atom, all things other than mind—whether near or far, past, future, or present—are clearly reflected in every state, like images in a mirror.

The *samatājñāna* (wisdom of equality) is that by which, having realized the equality of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) within the world thus reflected, one attains the immeasurable state of a mind that is always equal toward oneself and all sentient beings.

The knowledge of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) is that by which the Blessed One, while remaining thus in meditative equipoise and free from conceptual construction, nevertheless discerns the mental activities of all sentient beings through the sovereign power of his former vows and the merit of sentient beings.

The knowledge of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) is that by which one carries out the tasks for the world thus contemplated. This fourfold knowledge constitutes the perfection of realization; likewise, the Blessed One, the Omniscient One, perceives all of these directly. Furthermore, these five knowledges of the Blessed Vajradhara—which are individually realized and continuously occurring—stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect, just as the designation "one jar" occurs within the continua of atoms of form, taste, smell, and touch.

Because they are related through dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*), they exist inseparably and thus constitute the very object of the designation "a single sentient being. Likewise, regarding the five non-differentiated cognitions—the immeasurable and infinite Buddha-cognitions such as the powers (*bala*) and intrepidities (*vaiśāradya*)—which are non-conceptual and which continue simultaneously in their respective distinct forms, [the text states]: "Sentient beings are a single stream of consciousness" (*ekavijñānasantati*). This is because there is a simultaneous conceptualization of two [aspects] as a single sentient being within the unity of the mental consciousness-stream (*manovijñānasantati*).
Furthermore, the fact that these Buddha-cognitions possess the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of the five cognitions is explained in detail in the *Munimatālaṃkāra*.

Thus, the mirror-like cognition (*ādarśajñāna*) and the cognition of equality (*samatājñāna*), which is its support, constitute a single form because they both have the purified *dharmadhātu* as their object. The other two cognitions are also of a single flavor because they are solely dependent upon benefiting others and because they have suchness (*tathatā*) as their object. These two pairs [of cognitions] are not distinct in nature from the cognition of the purified *dharmadhātu*, because they have the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu* as their object through identity (*tādātmya*).
As it is said in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*:
In the purification of the *dharmadhātu*, the enjoyment of gnosis (*jñānasambhoga*) has the function of being mixed, thoroughly blended, and of a single flavor.

However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is simply the emptiness of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), such as the distinction or non-distinction of the five gnoses.

In that state, one is not disturbed by any conceptual constructions; thus, Akṣobhya is the nature of the purification of consciousness (*vijñāna*), whose essence is the gnosis of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*.
Because he shines and blazes due to the removal of all stains, Vairocana is the nature of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), whose form is the purity of form (*rūpa*).

Because he extends unsurpassed delight, Ratna is the nature of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), whose form is the purity of sensation (*vedanā*); he is Ratnasambhava because he arises with the nature of a jewel.

Because his nature consists in the discernment of immeasurable objects of knowledge, Amitābha has immeasurable radiance; he is the nature of the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), whose form is the purity of perception (*saṃjñā*).

Because his accomplishment is unfailing and fruitful due to its being the cause for establishing the welfare of the entire world, he is Amoghasiddhi; he is the nature of the purification of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) and consists of the wisdom of performing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Thus, there are five Buddhas who are the nature of the purification of the aggregates (*skandha*). Since emptiness alone is their reality, they possess the very nature of the sixth, Vajrasattva, by virtue of the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion.

And those beings who are born from the five Tathāgatas are the Bodhisattvas belonging to their respective families, such as Kṣitigarbha and others; they will be described as having the nature of the purification of the internal sense-bases (*adhyātmikāyatana*) by means of the verse beginning with "the eye is Mohavajrā. Furthermore, Rūpavajrā and the others have the nature of the purification of the external sense-bases, such as form and so forth; Locanā and the others have the nature of the purification of the elements, such as earth and so forth; and the Wrathful Ones, such as Yamārya and the rest, have the nature of the purification of faith and the other faculties.

For them as well, their nature is likewise that of Vajrasattva, just as waves consist of water. And it should be understood that these Tathāgatas and others are infinite because they arise in infinite forms through the power of the inclinations of infinite sentient beings who are attached to the aggregates and so forth, which are divided into immeasurable distinctions. Furthermore, it should be connected everywhere [with the following]: "The Tathāgatas and others residing in the state of purity, and the triple realm, are the Holder of the Vajra."

That which possesses the three realms—the desire, form, and formless realms—is the "three-realm" (*tridhātu*) mass of sentient beings; it too is likewise of the very nature of the Vajradhara of the causal tantra. And it is said: "The origin of all existence is everywhere.

This very one is the Holder of the Vajra (*vajradhṛk*). He is differentiated within himself by means of bliss and so forth, being divided by the distinctions of joy and the rest, and has the nature of innate great bliss (*sahaja-mahāsukha*); yet this is clearly realized by the disciple from the guru, for through the guru’s instruction, the glorious one should perceive reality through contact with wisdom (*prajñā*).
From the vajra-paryaṅka posture, one should observe the mind as having entered within the jewel.

Since it is thus, therefore, in this triangle—which is frequented by the Buddhas in the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which is pure because its single flavor is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and which has the shape of the letter *E* because of its triangular nature—[the syllable *ai*] is situated. "Of the delightful" means that it is a place of delight within the delightful; "denoted by the sound *e*" means that it is the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). By this, the navel-lotus and so forth are also indicated. In the center, upon the pericarp, is the syllable *vaṃ*, distinguished as the vajra-nature of skillful means (*upāya*). The connection is that just as there is a distinction internally, so it is obtained from the mouth of the Guru. And it is said:
The divine form of the solitary *kākā*, adorned in the center with the syllable *vaṃ*,
is the abode of all blisses and the jewel-casket of the Buddhas.
Thus [it is said]. It is called *divya* because one plays (*divyati*) therein.
He concludes: "The triangle," and so forth. *Vajra* is the *bola*, the conventional bodhicitta; its *āralli*—meaning its festival—is Vajrasattva, whose nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
(Note: This is the definition of *āralli*.)

For it is said in the *Rigyarallitantra*: "The goddess Rigī is Arallir Vajradhara. And in the *Vajrārallitantra*: "Vajrārallir is Vajrasattva. But in the *Sūtaka*, it is said that "Arallir is play (*krīḍā*)."

Thus, it is "supported" (*viniśrita*) by the *vajrāralli*; this support is the triangle. For this very reason, it is known here and in other tantras as the "source of phenomena" (*dharmodayā*), the "womb" (*yoni*), because it is the source of arising for the phenomenon of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and for the mandala which consists of all phenomena. The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), however, is as follows: the "source of phenomena" (*dharmodayā*) is so called because the arising—meaning the emergence—of the phenomena of the three vajras occurs within it through the nature of the Vajradhara of Great Bliss. It is the Dharmakāya, the primary body of Vajradhara. Furthermore, since the phenomena themselves possess that same nature, they are also the source of phenomena and the Dharmakāya.

It is called *bhaga* because great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is experienced within it. To state that this is not only the basis for the arising of great bliss but also for the entirety of speech—a point reached at this juncture—the author says, "Of that," and so forth. Here, "lotus" refers to the female and male [organs]. It has eight petals because the second maṇḍala consists of the eight channels (*nāḍī*). The ninth is the "bird-mouthed" channel; the pericarp is the *avadhūtī*. Within that lotus, its "bees" (*ali*) are the row (*paṅkti*), and the "bees" are the sixteen vowels.

For the conventional usage of relations and so forth follows the principal [element]. "Whose is Kāli? Kāli has thirty-four consonants; they are established" means in an unmanifest form. For at the time of utterance, the wind-born [sounds], being unmanifest by nature, arise in the lotus of the *bhaga* and become manifest through the articulatory organs such as the palate. As he will say: "The sound (*nāda*) is the mantra. But in the order of origination (*utpattikrama*), they are established in the form of letters (*lipi*). "Rites" refers to pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth. "Something" refers to the syllable (*akṣara*).

He states the eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*), beginning with *aka* and so forth. The *a*-group is the vowels (*āli*). *Ya-ra-la-va* is the *ya*-group. In the context of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), for the purpose of extracting mantras and the like, *śa-ṣa-sa-ha* alone are sometimes called the *śa*-group. However, the letter *kṣa* is not shown separately because it is a conjunction of *ka* and *ṣa*. Here, however, *śa-ṣa-sa-ha-kṣa* constitute the *śa*-group. Each of the groups beginning with *ka* consists of five letters. The "jewels" (*ratāni*) are attached to—that is, connected with—the groups; they are "equal," meaning they possess identical functions.
For whatever single syllable is intended by a yogin who is established in reality accomplishes [the goal]. Thus it is said in the *Dvikalpa*:
"Equal and of identical activity through the meditations on reality (*tattva*) that are of a single flavor (*samarasa*)."
"Equal" is said to mean "the same"; its wheel is traditionally known as the *rasa* (flavor).

The essence (*rasa*) of that which is equalized, its state as essence, is called the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). For this very reason, he says: "In the *vajrāralla*. The meaning is that [the letters] are equal only at the arising of the festival of great bliss, and not otherwise. Regarding "on each petal," since even fifty syllables arise within a single channel (*nāḍī*), there is no restriction of direction or petals for the arrangement of letters or groups of letters (*varga*) by one who contemplates the script. Due to the needs of those to be trained (*vineya*), there are occasional alternative explanations in certain tantras and other works. Thus ends the section on "the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*).

Because it illuminates the accomplishment of the Supreme Lord Vajrasattva through the cultivation of all phenomena as primordially unarisen, the letter *A* is declared to be the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), since it is the designation for the Perfection of Wisdom whose intrinsic nature is non-dual gnosis. Indeed, the letter *A* indicates the non-arising of all phenomena. And this very non-arising is the ultimate reality of all things—their true nature, their emptiness of self-characteristics, their lack of intrinsic being, and the purity of the gnosis of the Perfection.

In the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), it is because the syllable *A* is not produced from [the seed-syllable] of Vajrasattva in certain cases. Furthermore, it is "supreme" (*parama*) because it is the most excellent; it is "immutable" (*akṣara*) because its nature is the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the "supreme immutable" (*paramākṣara*), and the letter *A*, which illuminates that [body], is also the "supreme immutable. For this very reason, it is the best among all phonemes (*sarvavarṇaśreṣṭha*), either because it pervades all phonemes or because it is the foremost among all phonemes. As he will say: "Because it consists of the classes [of consonants]. And it is stated in the *Mañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti*: "It is the perfect radiance of all speech."
In the *Pañcakrama*:
"The entire statement would be short; it is neither manifold nor singular."

Because it is articulated through the very application of non-activity (*akāra*), it is not manifold. Because there is no differentiation in each [instance], it is not one. In ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), however, it is devoid of the nature of being either one or many. And because the welfare of all sentient beings is accomplished precisely through the sovereignty of the *dharmakāya*, there is great benefit from this; thus, it is "of great benefit" (*mahārtha*). Likewise, it is said in the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi*: [from the *Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi*].

“Guhyakādhipati, how do the Tathāgatas empower the mantra-system and the mantra-rituals with written syllables? In this regard, Guhyakādhipati, that speech which has been fully accomplished by the Tathāgatas over many thousands of eons—therein, Guhyakādhipati, a bodhisattva established in the letter ‘A’ should perform all activities. And so it is stated in the *Acalakalpa*: [Q/R] *Acalakalpa*
Having made the thought of awakening firm, the accomplishment of mantra is proclaimed;
otherwise, all ritual activities for the accomplishment of mantra are fruitless.
This is because, in brief, one contemplates that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
"Bodhicitta is indeed attained, and not otherwise; it would be nothing else. And in the *Āryamañjuśrītantra*:
[Q/R Mañjuśrītantra]

Endowed with ten gateways to the light of the Dharma, the hosts of gods become established in the practice of all mantras and practitioners of all mantras; they swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and all mantra-siddhis appear before them.

That is to say, by means of the worship of the Dharma—for the Tathāgatas are indeed the Dharma-body—when the Dharma is worshipped, all Tathāgatas, all Pratyekabuddhas, noble Śrāvakas, all Bodhisattvas, and all Mantras become well-established as if they themselves have been worshipped, and not by means of material worship. This is through the worship of practice: by acting for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, by engaging in the welfare of sentient beings, by not abandoning one's commitments, by not abandoning the activities of mantra-conduct, and by acting exactly as one has spoken.

By virtue of sharp wisdom, by virtue of an untiring mind, and by virtue of not abandoning the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), O friends, the Tathāgatas [are honored] up until the offering of material things (*nāmiṣapūjā*).

Alternatively, Vairocana is the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*); because he flows (*kṣarati*) in the form of the vajra-body of all Tathāgatas, he is [denoted by] the syllable *A*. Amitābha is [denoted by] the syllable *Ā*. Amoghasiddhi is the foremost of all colors because he possesses a manifold form (*viśvarūpa*) through all colors such as white, green, and so forth; thus he is the "Foremost of All Colors. Ratnasaṃbhava is the "Great Purpose" because from him—the source of the jewel that holds the wish-fulfilling gem—there arises the great benefit for all sentient beings.

Because he is the sovereign lord of the group beginning with Vairocana, the leader of the group is Akṣobhya; thus, the Supreme Lord, who consists of the five Buddhas, is the sixth. The syllable *a* likewise signifies him.

Having arisen within the hollow of the filaments (*kiñjalka*), he moves among the petals; therefore, he is said to be present even in the petals. Other syllables (*varṇa*) are likewise [treated]. For this very reason, in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), they too are described in some places as having the form of letters (*lipi*), to be meditated upon individually even within the hollow. However, the letter *A* is said to be their head. From that *A* alone, mantras and the accomplishments (*siddhi*) to be achieved through mantras arise. Why is this so? He says: "Because," and so forth. "All" refers specifically to those practitioners of the completion stage (*utpannakrama*).

Sound (*nāda*) is the unmanifest sound; the primary *nāda* is the syllable *A* itself. For this very reason, the scriptural form consisting of an upward stroke is called *nāda*. It is the "universal knot" (*viśvagranthi*) because it is the place of origin for all sentient beings; for this same reason, it is the "great abode" (*mahāsthāna*), as it provides space for many. It is the "womb" (*yoni*), the "pleasure-grove of Dharma" (*dharmāralli*), because the play (*vilāsa*) of the Dharma—namely, great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—occurs therein. To the question, "How is every expansion of speech a mantra?", he says: "Not [so]," and so forth. Therefore, the intention is that for one who has firm conviction in non-arising, everything is indeed mantra, since its intrinsic nature is unarisen.

Now he begins to explain the great significance of the syllable *e* and the others, starting with the words "Therefore," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the characteristic of arising from the *saṃpuṭa*": that by which the arising of Wisdom (*prajñā*) and Means (*upāya*) is characterized. "The Great Means" (*mahopāya*) refers to her form as the Perfection of Means (*upāyapāramitā*). She is "of universal form" (*viśvarūpā*) because she radiates through various emanations. She is "the object of all" (*viśvagocarā*) because, through the sovereign power of their merit and the impetus of their own vows, she is perceived by many fortunate beings (*bhavyasattva*), thus being their objective domain.

Because it is the place of birth for immeasurable sentient beings, the universal lotus is the *yoni*. For here, the *yoni* is the lower region of the navel of both woman and man; this very point has been stated in the passage beginning with "the universal knot" (*viśvagranthi*). We shall explain that for the yogin who is a male, it is also the source from which arise the forms of emanation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) that act for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings. "In the form of a vow" (*praṇidhirūpā*) means having the essential nature of the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhipāramitā*).

Regarding "Vajrakulā": because Vajra is Akṣobhya and she belongs to his family (*kula*), she is primary (*mukhyā*). However, this Prajñā should also be understood as belonging to the family of Ratnasaṃbhava in a secondary sense (*gauṇī*), thus she is one of the lineage of Ratnasaṃbhava. Regarding "Bālā": she is the Perfection of Power (*balapāramitā*). She is primary because, being the form of Vajratārā, she is sealed by Ratnasaṃbhava; thus, she is also of the Ratna family in a secondary sense. Because she is the form of Mṛtyuvañcanatārā, she is sealed by Vairocana and thus belongs to the Vairocana family. Because Kurukullā is sealed by Amitābha, she belongs to the Amitābha family.

Because she who has the form of Ekajaṭā is sealed by Akṣobhya, she also belongs to the Akṣobhya family. "By means of gnosis" refers to the perfection of gnosis (*jñānapāramitā*). Thus, these goddesses—Locanā and the others—are the embodiments of the purity of the elements, seals, measures, and perfections; through their nature as emptiness and compassion, they possess the essence of wisdom and skillful means, and are visualized within the wheels of emanation and so forth.

Thus, by means of the conviction that there is no difference between the signifier and the signified (*vācya-vācaka*), it is stated that through the generation stage (*utpatti-krama*), one visualizes [the deities] sometimes as having the very nature of the *evaṃ-maya* syllables, and sometimes as having the form of arms and so forth. He states another object signified by the two *evaṃ* syllables: "By the letter *e*, etc. One should have conviction that the upward-facing lotus of the navel and the downward-facing lotus of the head are the letter *e*, which is a triangle in the shape of the letter *e*, the very nature of Wisdom (*prajñā*).
The downward-facing heart-lotus and the upward-facing throat-lotus are circular in shape like the syllable *vaṃ*, having the nature of skillful means (*upāya*). As he will state:
"The wheel located at the head and the navel is situated in the form of the syllable *e*;
however, those situated at the heart and the throat are considered to resemble the syllable *vaṃ*."

At the time of union with a *caṇḍālī*, it shines through the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) that has the single flavor of bliss at the lotuses of the navel and heart, as well as at the lotuses of the throat and head, and subsequently at the pair of each [of these]. In this way, the syllable *E* is also the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), and so too is the syllable *Vaṃ*. Therefore, he says "in the syllable *E*" and so forth. Furthermore, wisdom is the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*) and means is the vajra; it shines through meditative absorption due to the arising of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Therefore, because [the tantra] has the nature of wisdom and method, which consist of emptiness and compassion, each individual [element] has the form of wisdom and method; this should be explained by repeating [the phrase]. Furthermore, in order to set forth another subject matter, he explains the opening statement with the words "Thus" (evam) and so forth. The connection is: "I speak thus. This is because [it begins with] "that which was heard by me. How does it indicate the entire collection of tantras?

Since the Blessed One—the Great Passion whose nature is wisdom and means, and whose form is great bliss—abides as the subject matter (*abhidheya*) in this tantra through a continuous, unceasing succession, it is logical that the tantra which expresses him is so designated. That which has been made an object by hearing it is "heard" (*śruta*). Is that merely the designation? No; for the Lord of Great Bliss is also heard. The meaning is that both the word and its referent together constitute the "Great Sentence" (*mahāvākya*) that is heard.

(164v/330) There would be non-difference, that is, no distinction; yet this is not the case. For at the very time when the listener and the compiler belong to a continuum (*saṃtāna*) non-different from the teacher, due to compliance with those to be trained (*vineya*), there is the absence of a distinct continuum. Alternatively, and so forth: the Dharma is what is to be taught; the "compiler" (*saṅgītikṛt*) is one who has compiled it. Regarding "that," and so forth: "That is I myself, the teacher and so on. "One" means singular. "Taste" (*rasa*) is a specific individual state (*bhāvaviśeṣa*). In which [state] the task for the sake of others is to be performed.

The meaning is that Vajradhara, though one alone, sports through various forms due to the differentiation of mental states (*bhāva*). This very statement is found here in this tantra; therefore, [the address] "O Blessed One" was used by the Blessed One.

He states another interpretation beginning with "the pledge" (*samaya*) and so forth. "Nose" (*nāsā*) refers to the *avadhūtī* in humans. For she is the nose of both "men," namely women and men; for even in the case of a man, [the central channel] is designated as the "nose" starting from the root of the *bola*. That itself is the "cavity" (*puṭa*). The drop of bodhicitta that arrives through its hollow is like a stream of milk. "Good time" (*sukāla*) means a favorable moment (*sukṣaṇa*), consisting of the nature of joy (*ānanda*) and supreme joy (*paramānanda*).

The *bindu* that has gone outside is like fire, burning with the sensation of suffering or with the experience of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, because of the burning [thought]: "Alas! Where is that bliss? It has reached inconceivability in the form of the fourth moment. To the question "How is it inconceivable?", he says: "Not," and so forth. Cessation—characterized by attachment, consisting of the three types of bliss due to the conceptualization of pleasure, and being the absence of bliss—is suffering or the sensation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.

For the Śrāvakas of middling capacity, liberation as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is not a real entity (*vastusad*), being of the nature of a negation through the exclusion of pleasure and so forth. For that [liberation] is not inferior, unlike the liberation of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). As it has been said: "A portion of existence belongs to those liberated according to the views of opponents."

It is "not supreme" as in the case of the perfectly awakened ones (*saṃbuddha*). It is said to be "unperceivable" because it has been established elsewhere that even conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*) there is nothing whatsoever that is a mere conceptual imputation (*prasajya-mātra*). However, passion (*rāga*) and dispassion (*virāga*), even though they are conventional, do not exist in the innate state (*sahajāvasthā*). Why? Because [the text says] "passion," and so forth. It is "unturbid" (*anāvila*) due to the absence of the defilement of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-kāluṣya*). Now, one might ask: since passion and dispassion are absent in the innate state, how can there be a state of "mixture"? To this he says:

The word "tathā" expresses unmixedness and oneness by virtue of being free from turbidity. For this very reason, it says "samarasa. One whose taste (*rasa*)—that is, whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—is equal is *samarasa*. And it is said in the *Dvikalpa*: "By this meaning, it is called *samarasa*, which is indeed a single state (*ekabhāva*)."

"Of one nature" means of a single essence. "By this meaning" refers to its being of the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). This is what is said: because of the experience of great bliss alone, the state of being mixed and the state of being one are designated for passion and non-passion merely by their not being experienced separately, just as with cyclic existence (*bhava*) and nirvāṇa. "Having a single flavor" (*samarasa*) also results from experiencing [reality] as the nature of non-conceptual great bliss. It is just as in the case of blue and other [colors]. For this very reason, he says: "It has a single flavor with all phenomena."

The Blessed One (*bhagavān*) alone is called "the one endowed with the [six] fortunes" (*samaya*). Sovereignty is independence; that belongs to the Blessed One because he has abandoned all obscurations along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*), and because it is characterized by the perfection of all qualities in every aspect. For the Blessed One, being free from obscurations, attains the unsurpassed and unobstructed excellence of body, speech, and mind, consecrated by the nectar of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). His form is complete, for his body is adorned with the supreme primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) of a great man.

Fame is complete because its sound resounds throughout all directions and intermediate points. Prosperity (*śrī*) is that by which one is sought after by many; it is characterized by an unsurpassed accumulation of merit. It is complete because it consists of all mundane and supramundane prosperity, being sought after through [the fulfillment of] desires. Knowledge is complete because, regarding every object of knowledge in its entirety and in all its aspects, it is pure, unattached, and unimpeded.

This speech is a complete effort, endowed with unsurpassed perfection of expression; it flows effortlessly, without attachment or interruption, and without exertion; it satisfies all the world according to their inclinations; it is equipped with all the components of musical tones; it is the liberator of the world; and because its activity is never interrupted through the enjoyment-body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*) and the emanation-body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*), it is constant in every aspect for the sake of others.

"Phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*) refers even to non-phenomena such as ignorance and so forth; they are called "phenomena" because they maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). "Accompanied by all the Tathāgatas and consorts" means accompanied by all the Tathāgatas and by the consorts beginning with Locanā. However, at the time of worship, all the Tathāgatas themselves are the consorts. Therefore, he says: "Aho hi," and so forth. For the sake of pleasing the Blessed One, the Vajra-holder, the Tathāgatas emanate their own bodies in the form of female deities corresponding to their respective virtues.

Furthermore, by means of the excellence of the superior female qualities produced through entry into the assembly of *vidyās*, they generate even greater satisfaction; thus, being included within the *vidyā* of Vajradhara, they worship Vajrasattva. They abide from the beginning of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) as their own essential nature, either in some cases in form or in meaning—as in [the passage] beginning with "In the secret... and so forth. They are pure because they express pure meanings;
for this very reason, through the cultivation of those meanings, the perfection of Buddhahood is achieved.

He explains: "By means of colors," and so forth. The further shore of saṃsāra is nirvāṇa. Because it is not within the sphere of experience of the śrāvakas and others, it is extremely remote; yet, being non-abiding, it does not abide in nirvāṇa.

(169v/340) He specifically explains Vajrasattva himself as "the inconceivable state. Regarding "by the Sugatas," the Sugatas here are the ten Bhūrbhujaḥ. They are distinguished from external *śaikṣas* and *aśaikṣas* because, although a possibility for them exists of returning [to cyclic existence] or of proceeding without remainder, they are praised [for being otherwise]. However, in every respect, this refers to the Blessed One. The connection is with the phrase "correctly characterized. It was stated that sentient beings (*sattvas*) and so forth are bound by afflictions such as delusion (*moha*).

"Correctly" means when that which is indeed the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion is characterized. For emptiness alone is the destroyer of all afflictions (*kleśa*). If wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) is practiced with an afflicted mind in its absence, there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāritva*), and from that, even an evil rebirth (*durgati*). Therefore, by abandoning the afflicted mind, one possesses a pure mind and pure wisdom-knowledge. How? Through the application of wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*), by means of awakening to the non-duality of emptiness and compassion.

Because, within the conventional external wisdom (*sāṃvṛtabahiḥprajñā*), that great bliss which is realized according to the instructions and through service is itself pure due to the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). It is the "truth" because its nature is emptiness; it is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); and it is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) because its essence is feeling (*vedanā*). That by which something is characterized is a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), namely the causal tantra (*hetutantra*). Through repeated absorption and cultivation, being transformed, it reaches the limit of excellence and becomes the transformation of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), due to the abandonment of the two along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanā*).

That which has the realization (*kāra*)—that is, the direct perception—of the activity consisting of emptiness and great bliss as its purity; which, in the ultimate sense, is equal to space and transcends the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of existence, non-existence, and so forth; yet, conventionally, illuminates the three worlds, as was stated previously—that is the *lakṣya* (the object to be characterized). That very same [object] is characterized by its defining marks (*lakṣaṇa*) when meditation reaches its peak, and even at the time of the defining marks, it is characterized through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*). However, it is difficult to characterize because, although it is somehow characterized by practitioners through the instructions of the Guru, it is [otherwise] hard to perceive.

It is "all-pervading" because it manifests as consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) even for the entire universe. Its "cause" (*hetu*) is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), which is the accumulation of gnosis (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*); its "condition" (*pratyaya*) is the cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), which is the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*) such as the application of wisdom (*prajñā-yoga*). It is "dependent on causes and conditions" because it is produced by these two when they are fully perfected. Through the radiation of diverse and immeasurable bodies and so forth, it accomplishes the welfare of beings according to their capacities. It is the "supreme among all worldly and transcendent accomplishments" (*siddhi*), the pinnacle of attainment, whose nature is the self-accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, and whose essential form is that of Vajradhara.
The connection should be made thus: "Vajradhara, the secret source of all tantras, is therefore completed.

The Blessed One is "Śrī" because of his possession of the unsurpassed accomplishment of the welfare of both self and others. He is also "Samputodbhava" (Born from the Union). And he himself, although free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*), acts for the benefit of sentient beings like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) through the sovereign power of his own vows and the merit of sentient beings. He is called "Kalpa" because he is conceived in such and such ways by sentient beings according to their respective inclinations (*adhimukti*). Thus it is said in the *Mahāsukhavajraguhyakalparāja*: [Q/R] *Mahāsukhavajraguhyakalparāja*

"However, because of the conceptualization for the sake of sentient beings from non-conceptual samādhi, it is therefore called 'kalpa' (an eon/creation) for the sake of the purification of conceptualization. Non-conceptual samādhi is the Blessed One. And in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
The non-conceptual knowledge of the Buddhas, however, is eternal.
Because it is non-conceptual, it is called "kalpa" [an eon] through its connection with conceptualization (*kalpanāt*).

And thus, because he shines forth with speed by means of his people, he is a *rājā* (king). The textual composition that expounds this is the *Śrīsaṃpuṭodbhavakalparāja*. By this, its superiority over other tantras is made known, since it alone reveals the unsurpassed and unique means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*). It is designated as "the first" because it is specified in relation to other *kalpas*. It is concluded, having been correctly grasped.
The fourth cluster in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*.
